after.problem: Find the critical points of the function $f(x)={e}^{{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}}.$
after.worked_solution:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}}) \\  & ={({x}^{3}-3{x}^{2})}^{′}{e}^{{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}} \\  & =(3{x}^{2}-6x){e}^{{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(3{x}^{2}-6x){e}^{{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${e}^{{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}}\ne 0$ for all $x,$ we can divide this equation by ${e}^{{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}}$ and solve the resulting equation. 

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-6x & =0 \\ 3x(x-2) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=0$ and $x=2.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists for all values of $x$ in the domain of $f(x).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ are $x=0$ and $x=2.$

after.problem: Find the critical points of the function  $f(x)={e}^{12x-{x}^{3}}?$
after.worked_solution:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{12x-{x}^{3}}) \\  & ={(12x-{x}^{3})}^{′}{e}^{12x-{x}^{3}} \\  & =(12-3{x}^{2}){e}^{12x-{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(12-3{x}^{2}){e}^{12x-{x}^{3}} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since ${e}^{12x-{x}^{3}}\ne 0$ for all $x,$ we can divide this equation by ${e}^{12x-{x}^{3}}$ and solve the resulting equation. 

$$
\begin{aligned}12-3{x}^{2} & =0 \\ 3(4-{x}^{2}) & =0 \\ (2-x)(2+x) & =0 \\ x & =-2,\,2\end{aligned}
$$

 
Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=-2$ and $x=2.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists for all values of $x$ in the domain of $f(x).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ are $x=-2$ and $x=2.$

after.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ If the critical points of $f(x)$ for $x\in (-\pi ,\pi )$ are $x={x}_{1}$ and $x={x}_{2},$ what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}?$
after.worked_solution:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡x & =-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =-\sqrt{3}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =-\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\sqrt{3})+n\pi  \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{3}+n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $-\pi <x<\pi .$

- setting $n=0$ gives $x=-\frac{\pi }{3}$

- setting $n=1$ gives $x=\frac{2\pi }{3}$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $-\pi <x<\pi .$ So, the solutions to this equation for $x\in (-\pi ,\pi )$ are 

$$
x=-\frac{\pi }{3},\,x=\frac{2\pi }{3}.
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=-\frac{\pi }{3}$ and $x=\frac{2\pi }{3}.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists for all values of $x\in (-\pi ,\pi ).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ for $x\in (-\pi ,\pi )$ are ${x}_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{3}$ and ${x}_{2}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=-\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot \frac{2\pi }{3}=-\frac{2{\pi }^{2}}{9}.
$$

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡x & =-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =-\sqrt{3}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =-\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\sqrt{3})+n\pi  \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{3}+n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $-\pi <x<\pi .$

- setting $n=0$ gives $x=-\frac{\pi }{3}$

- setting $n=1$ gives $x=\frac{2\pi }{3}$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $-\pi <x<\pi .$ So, the solutions to this equation for $x\in (-\pi ,\pi )$ are 

$$
x=-\frac{\pi }{3},\,x=\frac{2\pi }{3}.
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=-\frac{\pi }{3}$ and $x=\frac{2\pi }{3}.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists for all values of $x\in (-\pi ,\pi ).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ for $x\in (-\pi ,\pi )$ are ${x}_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{3}$ and ${x}_{2}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=-\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot \frac{2\pi }{3}=-\frac{2{\pi }^{2}}{9}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{x-2}{{x}^{2}+6}) \\  & =\frac{(x-2)^{′}\cdot ({x}^{2}+6)-(x-2)\cdot ({x}^{2}+6)^{′}}{({x}^{2}+6)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+6)-(x-2)\cdot 2x}{({x}^{2}+6)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+6-2{x}^{2}+4x}{({x}^{2}+6)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-{x}^{2}+4x+6}{({x}^{2}+6)^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{{x}^{2}-4x-6}{({x}^{2}+6)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x$ by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{{x}^{2}-4x-6}{({x}^{2}+6)^{2}} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-4x-6 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}-6 & =0 \\ (x-2)^{2}-4-6 & =0 \\ (x-2)^{2}-10 & =0 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =10 \\ x-2 & =\pm \sqrt{10} \\ x & =2\pm \sqrt{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists for all values of $x$ in the domain of $f(x).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.
